headline: Rope bridges let monkeys cross Amazon roads safely

sources.title: Good Good Good: Rope canopy bridges lead to 15,000 safe wildlife crossings
DailyGood: Amazon Canopy Bridges Lead to 15K+ Safe Road Crossings
Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute: How Brazil's Unique Canopy Bridges Are Saving Species
Brazilian monkeys cross highways using canopy bridges (video, CNN 10)

chunks.text: Monkeys in the Brazilian Amazon now {{cross over}} roads safely on rope bridges. The bridges are the work of a [[biologist]], the [[founder]] of a wildlife bridge project. In 2024, her team {{set up}} eight [[canopy]] bridges in the town of Alta Floresta. The project is [[in the news]] because it has reported more than 15,000 safe [[crossings]] in 15 months. Since the bridges went in, no animal has been killed on that [[stretch of road]].

verbs.correct: To go from one side to the other
verbs.wrong: To climb to the top of a tall tree
verbs.why: Hikers cross over a stream on a small wooden bridge, and children wait for the light before they cross over a busy street. Monkeys in the Brazilian Amazon now cross over roads safely on rope bridges strung between the trees.

verbs.correct: To install something in a place
verbs.wrong: To start a journey to a new place
verbs.why: Volunteers set up new bird boxes in a park, and a city sets up cameras at its busiest crossing. In 2024, the biologist's team set up eight canopy bridges over a road in Alta Floresta.

chunks.text: Roads {{cut through}} the forest, and animals of the [[treetops]] rarely {{come down}}. If the trees are too [[far apart]], a monkey crosses [[on foot]], and many get {{run over}}. The project estimates [[roughly]] 9 million [[mammals]] die on Brazilian roads each year. A canopy bridge lets monkeys {{keep away from}} traffic. Each has several [[layers]] of rope, since different [[species]] move differently: some [[leap]], some climb [[hand over hand]]. Two [[camera traps]] on each bridge {{pick up}} every crossing.

verbs.correct: To split a forest into two parts
verbs.wrong: To remove trees from an area
verbs.why: A new railway line can cut through a valley, and an old highway can cut through a wetland for miles. Roads cut through large areas of Amazon forest, leaving treetop animals with no safe way across.

verbs.correct: To move from a high place to the ground
verbs.wrong: To find something without looking for it
verbs.why: A cat finally comes down from the roof at dinner time, and squirrels come down to the ground to look for nuts. Many animals that live in the treetops rarely come down, so a road is a serious problem for them.

verbs.correct: To hit an animal with a car or truck
verbs.wrong: To use all of something until none is left
verbs.why: Drivers slow down so they do not run over the ducks, and a deer can get run over on a dark country road. Monkeys that try to cross on foot are the ones that get run over, and an estimated 9 million mammals die on Brazilian roads every year.

verbs.wrong: To move at the same speed as something
verbs.why: Signs tell visitors to keep away from the edge of a cliff, and parents tell children to keep away from a hot stove. A canopy bridge gives the monkeys a way to keep away from the traffic below.

verbs.wrong: To choose one thing from a group
verbs.why: A sensor can pick up movement near a gate at 3 a.m., and night cameras pick up animals that people never see. Two camera traps on each bridge pick up every animal that crosses.

chunks.text: The cameras in Alta Floresta have recorded spider monkeys, howler monkeys, and tamarins. It also {{turned out}} that monkeys were not the only users. When the team {{looked through}} the [[footage]], they found opossums, sloths, and mouse opossums crossing as well. The project says its goal is simple: a canopy bridge reconnects forest that a road has separated, and it reduces [[roadkill]].

verbs.correct: To be discovered to be true later
verbs.wrong: To refuse an offer or request
verbs.why: A strange noise in the attic can turn out to be a bird, and odd tracks in the snow can turn out to belong to a fox. It turned out that monkeys were not the only animals using the bridges.

verbs.correct: To examine many things one by one
verbs.wrong: To take care of an animal
verbs.why: A student looks through old maps in a library, and a photographer looks through hundreds of pictures to find the right one. When the team looked through the footage, they found opossums, sloths, and mouse opossums crossing as well.

chunks.text: Since 2021, the team has installed 32 bridges on another Amazon [[highway]]. Cameras there have recorded [[primate]] crossings for five years, and the total {{adds up to}} about 1,250. The team has also {{taken on}} roads in other parts of Brazil. Eight more are planned for Alta Floresta's [[urban area]], and the project hopes to {{branch out}} to other South American countries. The researchers say the pattern is simple: give animals a safe way across, and they use it.

verbs.correct: To reach a total of a certain amount
verbs.wrong: To make something bigger than before
verbs.why: Small donations can add up to more than a thousand dollars, and many short trips add up to a lot of driving. On another major Amazon highway, five years of recorded primate crossings add up to about 1,250.

verbs.correct: To agree to do a new piece of work
verbs.why: A cleanup group can take on two more beaches, and a busy builder cannot take on another house this year. The team has also taken on roads in other parts of Brazil.

verbs.correct: To extend work to new areas
verbs.wrong: To separate from a main road
verbs.why: A charity can start in one town and branch out across the whole region, and a company can branch out into three new countries. The project hopes to branch out to other countries in South America as well.

mainIdea.s: Rope bridges over an Amazon road have given monkeys and other animals more than 15,000 safe crossings. Researchers report no road deaths there and are building more bridges on other highways.
mainIdea.why: Cameras counted more than 15,000 safe crossings, no animal has been killed on that stretch of road, and more bridges are planned for other highways and other countries.

mainIdea.s: Brazil has cut roadkill across the whole country by hanging rope bridges above its highways. Researchers say the yearly total of 9 million road deaths has dropped sharply since 2024.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the zero-roadkill result is for one stretch of road in Alta Floresta. Nobody says the national figure of 9 million has fallen.

mainIdea.s: Scientists in the Brazilian Amazon have found a new species of titi monkey near a busy highway. They say the small animal lives only in a few small forest patches and is already at risk.
mainIdea.why: Spider monkeys, howler monkeys, and tamarins were all recorded on the bridges, but none of them is a new discovery. The news is about safe road crossings, not a new species.

lines.text: Did you see the story about the monkeys in Brazil? They {{cross over}} roads on rope bridges now.
Rope bridges for monkeys? Who builds something like that?

A biologist and her team. They {{set up}} eight of them over a road in the Amazon back in 2024. Since then the cameras have {{picked up}} more than 15,000 crossings, and no animal has been killed on that stretch of road.
[[Not a single one]]? That's impressive. But why do monkeys need a bridge in the first place?

Roads {{cut through}} the forest, and those animals almost never {{come down}} to the ground. If the trees are too far apart, they try to cross on foot, and that's when they get {{run over}}. An estimated 9 million mammals a year on Brazilian roads.
Nine million. [[I can't wrap my head around]] a number like that. So the bridge lets them {{keep away from}} the traffic completely.
Exactly. And it {{turned out}} monkeys aren't the only ones using them. When the team {{looked through}} the footage, they found sloths and opossums too.
[[The more the merrier]]. Are they stopping at eight bridges?
[[Not even close]]. They've {{taken on}} highways in other parts of Brazil, and they want to {{branch out}} to other countries in South America next.
[[Hats off to them]]. It all {{adds up to}} one simple idea: give animals a safe way across, and they'll use it.
